name: Provincial Population Distribution
description: Iran's provincial population distribution reveals substantial differences in settlement concentration and urbanization. Census comparisons provide a historical baseline, but provincial totals must be distinguished from city populations, population density, and migration.

seo.title: Iran's Provincial Population Distribution | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Understand Iran's provincial population patterns, census comparisons, urbanization differences, and the limits of historical regional data.

content.heading: A country of unequal population concentrations
content.content:
A provincial population map answers a particular question: how many residents were counted inside each administrative territory? It does not directly show how crowded settlements are, how accessible services are, or how many people live in the provincial capital. Iran's census publications distinguish provincial population totals from the national population-density indicator and from urban and rural residence. Those distinctions should remain visible when interpreting regional differences. [s1]

The selected census results identify Tehran as the largest provincial population concentration in 2016, followed by Razavi Khorasan, Esfahan, Fars, and Khuzestan. The table below follows three contrasting provinces across the published census comparisons. It is a selection illustrating changes in national population shares, rather than a complete provincial ranking. [s1]

content.title: Selected provinces' shares of Iran's population at two censuses

content.heading: Population size and settlement pattern are different
content.content:
The Stanford Iran 2040 study's analysis of the 2016 census emphasizes that provinces also differ in the balance between urban and rural residence. Qom, Tehran, Alborz, and Esfahan had comparatively small rural shares, whereas Sistan and Baluchestan, Golestan, and Hormozgan had comparatively large ones. A national urbanization figure therefore conceals quite different local settlement systems. [s2]

This matters when asking practical questions about population distribution. A provincial total alone cannot establish whether residents are concentrated in a metropolitan area or spread across smaller settlements. Likewise, a small share of the national population is not itself a measure of low population density: that requires an area denominator. Provincial comparisons should specify whether they concern residents, settlement categories, or people per unit of land. [s1][s2]

content.heading: What a changing share can establish
content.content:
Population share is a relative measure. A province can gain residents while losing national share if the country grows faster. Conversely, a rising share does not identify migration as the cause. The selected census tables document distribution; explaining the movement requires separate evidence on births, deaths, migration, and any administrative changes. [s1]

The historical comparisons are useful starting points for regional research, but they should not be relabeled as conditions in 2026. The Stanford study was published in 2017 and its geographical discussion principally interprets the preceding census. Its observations describe that historical baseline rather than an independently verified contemporary provincial distribution. [s2]

The most useful reading of the evidence is therefore layered: establish the census population, examine the urban–rural pattern, and investigate the mechanisms behind change. This preserves the difference between a documented geographical pattern and an explanation that still requires research. [s1][s2]

name: Household Change
description: Iran's census evidence records a long-term decline in average household size alongside changes in household composition. These changes involve childbearing, adult co-residence, marriage, and aging, and cannot be reduced to a single story about family life.

seo.title: Household Change in Iran | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Explore Iran's shrinking average household size, persistent adult co-residence, changing living arrangements, and census evidence limitations.

content.heading: Size is only one part of household change
content.content:
A household describes a living arrangement, while family relationships can extend beyond the people sharing a home. Research on Iran therefore examines both household size and composition: how many people live together, their relationships, and whether adult children or other relatives share the household. A smaller average does not by itself establish that extended-family ties have weakened. [s2]

The historical census series below documents a substantial decline in average household size. These are observations at particular censuses, with unequal gaps between them. They should not be read as annual measurements or as evidence that change followed a smooth path between census dates. [s1]

content.title: Average household size at selected censuses

content.heading: Fewer children did not mean fewer adults
content.content:
Aghajanian and Thompson's analysis of census evidence through 2006 found that falling household size reflected fewer child members alongside persistent adult co-residence. Their findings challenge a simple assumption that fertility decline must quickly produce a uniform household consisting only of parents and dependent children. Unmarried adult children and extended households remained important parts of the picture. [s2]

The authors distinguish possible explanations from established causes. Continued co-residence might reflect preferences for extended-family living, constraints on independent housing, or a combination. Their analysis does not settle the balance between choice and economic necessity. This distinction matters: the same household structure can arise from different circumstances, and a census roster cannot fully explain the decisions behind it. [s2]

content.heading: Aging adds another dimension
content.content:
An author-repository abstract for a separate study of older Iranians reports different living arrangements for men and women. Using historical census evidence, the researchers found that older men commonly continued living with a spouse, while solitary living increased among older women and co-residence with married children declined. These findings concern the historical populations studied; they are not a current estimate of older people's living arrangements. [s3]

The abstract also identifies unanswered questions about older people's social, economic, and health circumstances. Living alone should therefore not automatically be interpreted as either independence or isolation. The household roster establishes who shares a home; assessing support and vulnerability requires additional evidence. Only the abstract was accessible for this source, so detailed findings from the full article are not claimed here. [s3]

content.heading: Keeping different statistical sources separate
content.content:
A later study using Iran's Household Income and Expenditure Survey also reports declining household size and changes in household headship. That survey-based evidence supports further investigation beyond the census baseline, but its observations have not been appended to the census dataset here. Survey estimates and census tabulations need a definition and weighting check before they can form a comparable series. [s4]

The defensible conclusion is that household change involves several dimensions at once: average size, the presence of children and adults, relationships between members, and living arrangements in old age. A contemporary account needs updated evidence on each dimension rather than a single average presented as a complete portrait of Iranian families. [s2][s3][s4]

name: Migration
description: Migration connected with Iran includes internal residential movement, international study and employment, emigration, and displacement across borders. These processes require different evidence because census migration counts, student enrollment, migrant populations, and return movements measure different things.

seo.title: Migration in and from Iran | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Explore Iran's internal migration, international student mobility, diaspora questions, and Afghan returns while distinguishing incompatible measures.

content.heading: Several movements, several kinds of evidence
content.content:
Migration is not a single stream out of Iran. The country's census evidence records movement within national borders, while international sources examine study abroad and movements between Iran and Afghanistan. These subjects overlap in people's lives, but the statistics describe different populations and events. An internal residential move, enrollment overseas, and a monitored border return cannot be combined into one migration total. [s1][s3][s5]

The distinction also matters for the questions readers ask. A provincial migration table can describe where people moved within Iran during a defined interval. Student statistics can identify participation in education abroad. Border monitoring can document returns and deportations. None, on its own, supplies a complete account of how many people have permanently left Iran or of the size of an Iranian diaspora. [s1][s3][s4][s5]

content.heading: Internal migration extends beyond village-to-city movement
content.content:
Iran's historical urban transition makes rural-to-urban migration an important subject, but it is an incomplete description of more recent internal mobility. The KNOMAD report's background review, drawing on census research and UNFPA, identifies urban-to-urban movement as the dominant internal migration type by the later census intervals. A move between cities can cross a provincial boundary or remain within the same province. Settlement type and administrative boundary are separate classifications. [s2]

The Statistical Center's census summary distinguishes internal migrants moving between provinces from those moving within provinces. It also separates these categories from arrivals from abroad and an unknown category. These are observations for a census migration interval, not a count of every journey or a directly observed annual migration rate. [s1]

The UNFPA publication introducing its internal-migration study describes varied motives, including access to work and movement toward or away from urban settings. This range cautions against assuming that all moves have the same purpose or direction. The publication introduces a study focused on the historical census interval; its introductory description does not establish the prevalence of each motive today. [s6]

content.title: Two separate ways to classify an internal move
content.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A["Internal residential move"] -->|"Classify administrative boundary"| B["Within one province"]
  A -->|"Classify administrative boundary"| C["Between provinces"]
  A -->|"Classify origin and destination settlements"| D["Urban to urban"]
  A -->|"Classify origin and destination settlements"| E["Rural to urban"]
  A -->|"Classify origin and destination settlements"| F["Urban to rural"]
  A -->|"Classify origin and destination settlements"| G["Rural to rural"]
```
content.summary: The branches represent alternative classification dimensions, not additive groups. A move can belong to one administrative category and one settlement category simultaneously.

content.heading: Study, skilled migration, and diaspora are distinct questions
content.content:
UNESCO defines international student mobility around physically crossing a national border for education in a destination different from the student's country of origin. Its guidance distinguishes this from simply holding foreign citizenship. Country of origin may be operationalized through prior education or residence, depending on available reporting. Consequently, a count of Iranian citizens at foreign universities and a count of internationally mobile students from Iran may not be identical. [s3]

Student enrollment abroad also does not establish permanent emigration. Measuring graduate retention or return requires evidence after study. Similarly, a defensible assessment of skilled migration needs explicit educational or occupational criteria and a defined period; an enrollment count cannot supply those missing dimensions. Diaspora research raises another boundary question: whether the population includes only people who migrated or also descendants. These questions remain research requirements here rather than grounds for an unsupported headline total. [s3][s4]

content.heading: Afghan returns require attention to coercion
content.content:
UNHCR's border-monitoring report for 2025 documents returns from Iran that included deportations and departures under adverse circumstances. It describes restrictive policies, deteriorating conditions, and protection risks following return. The label 'return' therefore should not be read as proof that departure was freely chosen or that arrival in Afghanistan resolved protection needs. [s5]

A subsequent response plan describes pressure on reception systems and communities receiving returnees, including demands on housing, services, and employment. Its planning expectations must remain separate from completed movements. Together, these documents show why migration reporting needs both a clearly defined measure and an account of the circumstances behind it. A border-flow report cannot substitute for a resident-population estimate, and an operational forecast cannot be presented as an observed outcome. [s4][s5][s7]
